meta.description: Textbook BFS with std::queue<pair<int,int>> (deque) and vector<vector<int>> dist; no div/mod per pop.
Queue is a std::list<pair<int,int>> (one heap node per cell) plus a bit-packed vector<vector<bool>> visited array.
Dijkstra with a binary heap of (dist,r,c) tuples on the unit-weight grid instead of a FIFO queue.
Bit-parallel BFS: every level recomputes the frontier for the whole grid with 64-bit word ops (~4000 full sweeps, no queue).
Distances in an unordered_map<int,int> keyed by cell id (count + operator[] per neighbour) instead of a flat array.
Two hash tables: unordered_set<long long> visited plus unordered_map<long long,int> dist, 64-bit keys.
TOO SLOW: std::map<pair<int,int>,int> distances, a red-black-tree walk over millions of nodes per lookup.
Bellman-Ford over the raw edge list with early exit: a few sequential passes over all edges with random dist reads/writes, no heap.
Same lazy binary-heap Dijkstra, but vector<vector<pair>> adjacency grown by push_back, vector<bool> done, getchar_unlocked reader.
std::set<pair<ll,int>> as an indexed priority queue (erase + reinsert on improvement), vector<vector<pair>> adjacency.
Standard lazy binary-heap Dijkstra with scanf input for all 1.8M numbers and vector<vector<pair>> adjacency.
The intended CSR + heap algorithm, but cin left synchronised with stdio (no sync_with_stdio(false)).
std::map<int,vector<pair>> adjacency plus unordered_map dist and unordered_set done (tree + hash lookups instead of arrays).
TOO SLOW: std::map adjacency, std::map dist, std::set done, std::set as the PQ, and cin synced with stdio.
Single DP row updated in place with a saved diagonal and branch-free max, scanf into char buffers.
Full (n+1)x(m+1) uint16_t table in one flat 128 MB array instead of two rolling rows (streaming writes).
Full vector<vector<uint16_t>> table filled column by column: the inner loop strides across 8000 rows (a new page per access).
Top-down memoised recursion lcs(i,j) over a vector<vector<short>> memo (recursion depth up to n+m).
Hunt-Szymanski: LIS over all ~16M matching (i,j) pairs, one lower_bound on the threshold vector per pair.
Materialises all ~16M matching pairs in a vector, std::sorts them by (i asc, j desc), then patience-sorting LIS.
TOO SLOW: each DP row is a fresh unordered_map<int,int> 'sparse array', copied into prev (prev = cur) every row.
Iterative bottom-up segment tree (2n array) with an fread reader and a hand-rolled integer writer.
Generic range-add/range-sum two-BIT template used for point updates: O(n log n) build, both trees touched per operation.
Square-root decomposition: O(sqrt n) per query summing partial blocks element-wise and whole blocks via block sums.
The intended Fenwick tree, but cin/cout (sync off) with endl after each answer: one write(2) per query.
Classic recursive top-down segment tree (4n array) with scanf input and a printf per answer.
Segment tree of heap-allocated nodes linked by pointers (new per node), cin input.
TOO SLOW: the intended Fenwick tree stored in a std::map<int,long long> used as a sparse array.
Shift-And (bitap): one shift/OR/AND per text character on a 64-bit state, KMP fallback for patterns longer than 64.
KMP compiled into a 256-column DFA: one dependent table load per character (no fallback loop); fread input.
Rabin-Karp with a hash modulo 2^61-1 (128-bit multiplies), every hash hit confirmed with memcmp.
Z-function over pattern + '#' + text: a 20M-entry int array and a second pass to collect matches.
The intended KMP, but cin left synchronised with stdio, so the 20 MB text is read through stdio char by char.
Brute force with t.substr(i, m) == p at every position: one heap-allocated 24-char temporary per text position.
TOO SLOW: 'Rabin-Karp' recomputing each window's hash mod 1e9+7 from scratch (O(n*m)), hits verified exactly.
Offline: sort values and (query, index) pairs, two-pointer sweep, answers printed in input order with printf.
Hand-written recursive merge sort copying both halves into fresh vectors at every level, hand-written binary search, printf.
Values in a std::list sorted with list::sort (merge sort over scattered nodes), copied to a vector for upper_bound.
Same sort + upper_bound with cin/cout (sync off) and endl after every answer: one write(2) per query.
Same sort + upper_bound with cin/cout left synchronised with stdio ('\n', no endl).
__gnu_pbds order-statistics red-black tree over (value, index) pairs; order_of_key per query.
TOO SLOW: sqrt-decomposition template with sorted blocks of size sqrt(n log n); each query binary-searches all ~160 blocks.
No DFS: BFS from the root records order/parents/depths, subtree sizes accumulated over the reversed order.
Iterative preorder with std::stack<pair<int,int>> over vector<vector<int>> adjacency, sizes summed in reverse preorder.
Recursive DFS (depth 1e6) over vector<vector<int>> adjacency with scanf input.
Recursive DFS over vector<set<int>> adjacency: every neighbour is a separately allocated tree node.
Recursive DFS over unordered_map<int, vector<int>> adjacency: a hash lookup plus a heap vector per vertex.
Both edge directions in one std::multimap<int,int>; recursive DFS enumerates neighbours with equal_range (tree search per vertex).
TOO SLOW: 'graph as a map of sets' (map<int,set<int>>), std::map of subtree sizes, recursive DFS, cin synced with stdio.
